Raised from 1645 for the fifth Dalai Lama on Lhasa's Red Hill, its 13 storeys contain more than 1,000 rooms, and its Red Palace holds the gilded burial stupas of eight Dalai Lamas.

The 452-metre twins were the world's tallest buildings from 1998 to 2004 and are joined at the 41st and 42nd floors by a two-storey skybridge that is deliberately not fixed rigidly to either tower, so it can slide as they sway.
Finished in 1609, its six-storey white keep has survived earthquakes and war; in the 1945 air raid on Himeji an incendiary bomb landed on its top floor and failed to explode.
The shrine's 16-metre vermilion torii, rebuilt in camphor wood in 1875, stands in the Seto Inland Sea and seems to float at high tide; the shrine buildings themselves stand on piers over the water.
Its Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests is a 38-metre circular wooden hall, first built in 1420 and rebuilt in 1890 entirely without nails, where emperors prayed at the winter solstice.
Built around AD 850, the complex once held some 240 temples; its central temple to Shiva rises 47 metres, ringed by reliefs telling the Ramayana.

Founded in 1782 when Bangkok became Siam's capital, its Temple of the Emerald Buddha guards a 66-centimetre jadeite Buddha whose gold robes the king personally changes three times a year with the seasons.

Finished in 1616 for Sultan Ahmed I, it is lined with more than 20,000 hand-made Iznik tiles; its six minarets matched the number at Mecca, and tradition says a seventh was then built at Mecca to restore the difference.

Some 30 pharaohs added to it over 1,500 years; the great hypostyle hall's 134 columns cover an area big enough to hold Notre-Dame Cathedral, and one of Hatshepsut's obelisks still stands at 29 metres.

Beneath its Temple of the Inscriptions, archaeologists found the tomb of King Pakal in 1952, the king wearing a mosaic death mask of jade and a sarcophagus lid carved with his fall into the underworld.
Its castle, El Castillo, tops a 12-metre cliff and is thought to have worked as a lighthouse: two small windows align with the only gap in the reef, guiding Maya trading canoes in to shore.
Its Hieroglyphic Stairway carries more than 2,200 carved glyphs across 63 steps, the longest single inscribed text the Maya left behind.
This oasis city grew rich taxing Silk Road caravans between Rome and Persia; in the 270s AD its queen Zenobia seized Rome's eastern provinces and briefly ruled an empire of her own.
The Temple of Jupiter's podium includes three stones of about 800 tons each, among the largest ever moved, and six of its original 54 columns still stand, each over 20 metres tall.
Its Great Enclosure wall runs about 250 metres and stands up to 11 metres high, laid entirely without mortar; from here Shona kings traded gold that reached as far as China in the 1400s.
The world's largest mud-brick building, its three great towers are each topped with an ostrich egg; every year the town replasters the whole mosque by hand in a single-day festival.

Founded around 880, the castle complex covers some 70,000 square metres, the largest ancient castle in the world; St Vitus Cathedral inside it was under construction, on and off, for nearly 600 years.
Court astrologers chose the moment to lay its foundation stone: 5:31 on 9 July 1357, a sequence of odd numbers picked for luck; the 30 statues lining its 516 metres were added centuries later.
Begun in 1248 and only finished in 1880, faithfully to the original medieval plan, its twin spires reach 157 metres and briefly made it the tallest building in the world.

The Habsburgs' summer seat holds 1,441 rooms; in 1762 a six-year-old Mozart performed here for Empress Maria Theresa, and legend says he proposed marriage to the young Marie Antoinette after slipping on its polished floor.

Completed in 1894, its two bascules of more than 1,000 tons each still lift around 800 times a year for river traffic and open in about a minute; the red, white and blue paint dates from the 1977 Silver Jubilee.
William the Conqueror raised its White Tower from 1078; the fortress has served as royal palace, prison and menagerie, and Anne Boleyn and Catherine Howard were both executed on its green.
Queen Victoria was the first monarch to live here, moving in in 1837; the palace has 775 rooms, and its east front, the face everyone photographs, was only added in 1913.
Consecrated in 1065, it has hosted every English coronation since William the Conqueror's in 1066; Geoffrey Chaucer's burial here in 1400 began its Poets' Corner.
Daniel Chester French's seated Lincoln is 5.8 metres of Georgia marble; the 36 Doric columns around the memorial stand for the 36 states in the Union when Lincoln died.

The world's tallest stone obelisk at 169 metres; work stopped for 23 years in the Civil War era, and the marble visibly changes shade about 46 metres up, where building resumed from a different quarry.
At 553 metres it was the world's tallest freestanding structure for 32 years; its glass floor, installed in 1994, is rated to hold the weight of 41 polar bears.
Poured in the mid-1930s, its concrete would pave a two-lane road from San Francisco to New York; the dam stands 221 metres tall and holds back Lake Mead, the largest US reservoir by capacity.
The East Side Gallery is a 1.3-kilometre stretch of the Wall painted by 118 artists in 1990; its most famous panel, Dmitri Vrubel's Fraternal Kiss, shows Brezhnev and Honecker mid-embrace.
This 396-metre granite spike guards the entrance to Guanabara Bay; its cable car has run since 1912, only the third built anywhere, and it doubled as a film set for the Bond film Moonraker in 1979.
Ivan the Terrible ordered it built in 1555 after capturing Kazan; nine chapels with patterned onion domes cluster around a central 47-metre tent-roofed tower.
Thirty rock-cut caves in a horseshoe cliff, painted between the 2nd century BC and AD 480, were abandoned and forgotten until a British hunting party stumbled on them in 1819.
The Kailasa temple here was carved from the top down out of a single basalt cliff in the 8th century; workers removed an estimated 200,000 tons of rock to free the finished temple from the stone.
Capital of the Vijayanagara Empire and one of the richest cities of its age around 1500, its Vittala Temple holds 56 stone pillars tuned to ring like bells when struck.

clue: Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque, United Arab Emirates 🇦🇪
fact: Finished in 2007 and able to hold more than 50,000 worshippers, its main hall carpet is the largest hand-knotted carpet in the world at 5,627 square metres, woven by 1,200 artisans.

At 6,961 m (22,837 ft) Aconcagua is the highest mountain outside Asia and the tallest in both the Western and Southern Hemispheres. Despite the altitude its normal route is a walk-up needing no technical climbing, though its weather kills climbers most seasons.

Flash floods rushing through a crack in Navajo sandstone polished this slot canyon into flowing waves of red rock. Around midday in summer, shafts of sunlight fall straight to the floor of Upper Antelope Canyon, on Navajo land near Page and visitable only on guided tours.

New Zealand's highest mountain at 3,724 m, called Aoraki, 'cloud-piercer', in te reo Māori. A huge rock avalanche in 1991 sheared about 10 m from its summit, and ice and rock loss has lowered it since.

The driest non-polar desert on Earth: some of its weather stations have never recorded rain, and its hyper-arid core averages under 15 mm a year. The same clear, dry skies put the ALMA observatory's 66 radio antennas on its Chajnantor plateau, 5,000 m up.

Fundy's tides are the highest on Earth, rising as much as 16 m at Burntcoat Head, as much water as all the world's rivers combined pours in and out twice a day. At the Hopewell Rocks, flowerpot sea stacks stand on an ocean floor you can walk at low tide.

Not a canyon at all, but a row of amphitheatres bitten into the Paunsaugunt Plateau, filled with pink limestone spires called hoodoos. At 2,400-2,700 m elevation, some 200 freeze-thaw cycles a year wedge the rock apart grain by grain.

Erosion carved compressed volcanic ash into 'fairy chimney' spires, and people carved back: the soft tuff holds rock-cut churches and whole underground cities such as Derinkuyu, which descends about 60 m. At dawn, fleets of hot-air balloons drift over the valleys of Göreme.

The Big Room, roughly 1,200 m long and up to 79 m high, is among the largest cave chambers in North America. On summer evenings some 400,000 Brazilian free-tailed bats spiral out of the Natural Entrance in a column that can take three hours to empty.

The world's largest inland body of water at about 371,000 km² is a lake in all but name: the Volga makes its northern third nearly fresh while the south is almost as salty as the ocean. Its surface sits about 28 m below sea level.

A boss of fluted igneous columns rising 386 m above the Belle Fourche River, formed as an intrusion that cooled and cracked into hexagons underground and was exposed by erosion. Proclaimed the first US national monument in 1906, it is Bear Lodge, sacred to the Lakota and other Plains tribes.

The Eiger's 1,800 m north wall was the last of the Alps' great north faces to be climbed, in 1938, after a run of fatal attempts earned it the nickname Mordwand, 'murder wall'. A cog railway tunnels through the mountain itself, with windows cut into the face.

A cold desert of gravel plains and bare rock where winter brings -40 °C and herders' camels grow shaggy coats. At Bayanzag's Flaming Cliffs in 1923, Roy Chapman Andrews' expedition found the first dinosaur eggs recognised by science.

Between Guilin and Yangshuo the Li River threads a forest of limestone towers, the karst landscape printed on China's 20-yuan banknote. The towers are the eroded floor of a tropical sea that covered the region some 300 million years ago.

Granite pinnacles, gnarled pines gripping bare rock, and seas of cloud made Huangshan the model for classical Chinese shan shui painting. More than 60,000 stone steps stitch its paths together, and porters still carry loads up them slung from bamboo shoulder poles.

The Potaro River pours over a sheer 226 m ledge in Guyana's rainforest, making Kaieteur the largest single-drop waterfall on Earth by volume, about five times Niagara's height. No road reaches it: visitors arrive by small plane or a trek of several days.

A 900,000 km² sea of red sand that is only semi-desert: summer rains green it enough for great herds and the black-maned Kalahari lions. The Okavango River ends here, spreading into an inland delta instead of ever reaching the sea.

Among the world's most active volcanoes, Kīlauea erupted almost continuously from 1983 to 2018 at Puʻu ʻŌʻō. The 2018 lower East Rift eruption destroyed more than 700 homes, and the summit's Halemaʻumaʻu crater periodically hosts a roiling lava lake.

North America's largest alpine lake by volume is 501 m deep and famed for cobalt clarity, with visibility sometimes past 20 m. It straddles the California-Nevada line, its surface 1,897 m up in the Sierra Nevada, and despite hard winters it never freezes over.

The world's longest freshwater lake (about 673 km) and second deepest at 1,470 m, holding roughly 16% of Earth's unfrozen surface fresh water. Its clear waters evolved more than 250 species of cichlid fish found almost nowhere else.

The world's largest volcanic lake fills the caldera of a super-eruption about 74,000 years ago that may have cooled the planet for years. Samosir Island, uplifted from the caldera floor, is nearly the size of Singapore and home to the Christian Batak people.

The longest known cave system on Earth, with more than 676 km (420 miles) of surveyed passages and more still being mapped. Gypsum crystals coat its dry upper levels, while the Echo River, home to blind white fish, runs through its depths.

The largest volcano on Earth by volume: it rises 4,169 m above the sea and about 17 km from its base on the ocean floor, a taller pile than Everest. On its northern flank the Mauna Loa Observatory has measured atmospheric CO₂ since 1958, producing the Keeling Curve.

A dormant twin-coned volcano: Greater Ararat (5,137 m) is Turkey's highest peak, and tradition holds that Noah's Ark came to rest on it. It stands in Turkey but is Armenia's national symbol, printed on its coat of arms and visible from Yerevan on clear days.

Greece's highest summit, Mytikas (2,917 m), was the throne of the twelve Olympian gods, its peak usually hidden by cloud. Nobody is known to have stood on top until 1913; the massif is now a national park famed for its wildflowers and chamois.

The most glaciated peak in the contiguous United States, wrapped in 26 named glaciers, and the most topographically prominent: it rises about 4,000 m from the surrounding lowlands. It is an active volcano whose mudflows (lahars) threaten towns in the Puyallup valley below.

A tepui whose flat summit, about 31 km², is ringed by cliffs up to 1,000 m tall at the junction of Venezuela, Brazil and Guyana. It inspired Conan Doyle's 'The Lost World'; its blackened summit rocks host a tiny frog that, unable to hop well, curls into a ball and rolls away from danger.

On 18 May 1980 its north flank slid away in the largest landslide in recorded history, and the eruption that followed cut the summit from 2,950 m to 2,549 m. A new lava dome has been growing inside the horseshoe crater ever since, most recently in 2004-2008.

Tambora's April 1815 eruption, the largest in recorded history, blasted about 1,000 m off the summit and left a caldera 6 km wide. Its stratospheric sulphur veil caused 1816, the 'Year Without a Summer', with crop failures and famine across the northern hemisphere.

The highest mountain in Antarctica at 4,892 m, it was first sighted from the air in 1958 and not climbed until 1966. It crowns the Sentinel Range of the Ellsworth Mountains, roughly 1,200 km from the South Pole, where summer temperatures hover near -30 °C.

Often called the world's oldest desert, arid for at least 55 million years, it runs some 2,000 km along Namibia's Atlantic coast. At Sossusvlei its apricot dunes exceed 300 m, among Earth's tallest, and fog rolling in off the ocean keeps its desert life alive.

One of the world's largest inland deltas: floodwater from Angola fans out into the Kalahari and evaporates rather than reaching any sea. The flood peaks in the dry winter, drawing one of Africa's densest concentrations of elephants, lions and wild dogs to the shrinking lagoons.

At 4,884 m, Puncak Jaya (the Carstensz Pyramid) is the highest point between the Himalayas and the Andes and the highest island peak on Earth. Glaciers beside this equatorial summit, extensive in the 1930s, have shrunk to a few remnants expected to vanish within years.

Europe's most powerful waterfall: about 600 tonnes of water per second pour over a 23 m ledge spanning 150 m. The falls formed roughly 15,000 years ago as the Rhine was diverted into a new channel at the end of the last ice age.

The Empty Quarter is the largest continuous sand desert on Earth, some 650,000 km² of dunes up to 250 m high across four countries. Parts of its interior can go a decade without rain; Wilfred Thesiger's camel crossings of the 1940s remain its benchmark journeys.

The largest hot desert on Earth at about 9.2 million km², nearly the size of the United States, spread across 11 countries. Its sand seas cover only about a quarter of it; most of the Sahara is gravel plain and rock plateau, and the dunes of Erg Chebbi in Morocco rise some 150 m.

Santorini's crescent is the rim of a volcano that drowned its own centre: the eruption of around 1600 BCE buried the port of Akrotiri and is a candidate source for the Atlantis story. The dark islets in the bay, Nea Kameni, are new lava domes that last erupted in 1950.

This Aeolian island erupts in small explosions every few minutes and has done so for centuries, earning it the name 'Lighthouse of the Mediterranean'. Its Sciara del Fuoco, a vast scar down the northwest flank, funnels lava flows straight into the Tyrrhenian Sea.

A trough of swirled red-and-cream sandstone in Arizona's Coyote Buttes, sculpted by wind and water from dunes laid down some 190 million years ago. Access is by lottery only, a few dozen hikers a day, and there is no trail: visitors navigate by photo guide and GPS.

Five leaps totalling 948 m down the Drakensberg's Amphitheatre wall make the Tugela usually the world's second-tallest waterfall, and some surveys argue it edges past Angel Falls. The flow is seasonal: after summer rains it streams, in dry winters it thins to a thread.

Europe's grandest canyon: limestone walls up to 700 m high above a river turned milky turquoise by glacial flour. The gorge was unknown to outsiders until Édouard-Alfred Martel's 1905 expedition traversed it in wooden boats; its cliffs are now a cradle of sport climbing.

The Nile is conventionally measured at 6,650 km from the Kagera River, its farthest headstream, which rises in Burundi and drains through Lake Victoria. On its way north the White Nile spreads into the Sudd of South Sudan, one of the world's largest wetlands, where about half its water is lost to evaporation.

The Amazon discharges about 209,000 cubic metres of water per second, more than the next seven largest rivers combined. At Manaus its blackwater Rio Negro tributary runs beside the muddy main stem for over 6 km at the Meeting of Waters without mixing.

At about 6,300 km the Yangtze is Asia's longest river. The Three Gorges cut up to 300 m deep through limestone west of Yichang, and the cliffs of Qutang Gorge, the shortest and most dramatic of the three, now rise out of the Three Gorges Dam reservoir.

The Mississippi drains all or part of 32 US states, about two-fifths of the country's land area. At Memphis it runs over a kilometre wide below the bluffs, crossed by three road and rail bridges to the Arkansas shore.

The Congo is the world's deepest river, with measured depths over 220 m in its lower reaches. It is the only major river to cross the equator twice, looping north of it around the Congo Basin before swinging south again on its way to the Atlantic.

More than 400 million people live in the Ganges basin, the most populous river basin on Earth. At Varanasi, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, more than 80 ghats, broad stone steps for bathing and ceremony, line its western bank.

The Danube flows through ten countries, more than any other river, and past four capitals: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade, a record no other river matches. In Budapest it splits around Margaret Island, with the Parliament building standing directly on its Pest bank.

The Yenisei is the largest river flowing into the Arctic Ocean, discharging about 19,600 cubic metres of water per second. At Krasnoyarsk it runs almost a kilometre wide beneath the Communal Bridge, and in spring its breaking ice jams back water up for kilometres upstream.

The Yellow River carries more silt than any other major river, historically about 1.6 billion tonnes a year, most of it loess washed off the plateau it crosses. At Hukou its whole muddy flow squeezes into a gorge barely 30 m wide and pours over a ledge, the largest waterfall on the river.

The Amur forms about 1,600 km of the border between Russia and China. At Khabarovsk the Ussuri joins it from the south, and the combined road-and-rail bridge carrying the Trans-Siberian Railway across the river is over 2,500 m long.

Each monsoon the Mekong pushes so much water up Cambodia's Tonlé Sap channel that the great lake at its end expands to several times its dry-season area, a seasonal flow reversal. Its basin lands about 2 million tonnes of wild fish a year, the largest inland fishery on Earth.

The Mackenzie is Canada's longest river and drains about a fifth of the country. At Fort Simpson it is joined by the Liard River, and its delta on the Beaufort Sea is scattered with thousands of lakes and pingos, ice-cored hills that grow out of the permafrost.

The Lena ends in a delta about 400 km wide holding more than 1,500 islands, the largest delta on the Arctic coast. Upstream, the Lena Pillars, weathered limestone towers up to 100 m high, line its bank for tens of kilometres south of Yakutsk.

The Niger runs in a great boomerang bend, flowing northeast into Mali before turning sharply south at the edge of the Sahara. Around Djenné and Mopti its inland delta floods each year to roughly the size of Belgium, then slowly drains as the river falls.

At 3,530 km the Volga is Europe's longest river, and about half of Russia's river freight still moves on it. It meets the Kama, its largest tributary, just below Kazan, and past Volgograd it spreads into the Akhtuba floodplain and a broad Caspian delta.

When gold was found on the Klondike in 1896, Dawson City at its meeting with the Yukon boomed to some 30,000 people within two years. Yukon chinook salmon still swim as far as 3,000 km inland to spawn, among the longest salmon migrations in the world.

The Indus gave India its name, from the Persian word for this river. Mohenjo-daro, one of the largest cities of the Bronze Age, stood on its Sindh plain, and the Lloyd Barrage at Sukkur, completed in 1932, remains one of the largest irrigation works in the world.

The Zambezi pours over a basalt lip 1,708 m wide at Victoria Falls, the largest sheet of falling water on Earth. Below the falls it is dammed twice, at Kariba and Cahora Bassa, two of the largest reservoirs in the world by volume.

Measured up the Irtysh, the Ob system runs about 5,410 km, the longest river system in Asia. At Khanty-Mansiysk the Irtysh meets the Ob and the two run side by side, dark water beside pale, for kilometres before they finally blend.
The world's most visited museum began as a 12th-century fortress; I. M. Pei's glass pyramid, opened in 1989 as its main entrance, stands about 21 metres tall in the Cour Napoléon.

clue: Metropolitan Museum of Art, United States 🇺🇸
fact: The largest art museum in the Americas holds some 1.5 million objects; its glass-walled Sackler Wing houses the Temple of Dendur, a complete Egyptian temple of about 15 BC that Egypt gave to the United States.

Free to all since it opened in 1759, it holds about eight million objects, among them the Rosetta Stone, on display here since 1802. Its Great Court, roofed in glass in 2000, is the largest covered public square in Europe.

Founded by Pope Julius II in 1506, the museums run through some 7 km of galleries and end at the Sistine Chapel, whose ceiling Michelangelo painted between 1508 and 1512 on a scaffold he designed himself.

Catherine the Great founded it in 1764 with a purchase of 225 paintings; it now holds around three million items, and a team of cats, on staff since an imperial decree of 1745, guards the Winter Palace cellars against rats.

Built as a railway station for the 1900 World's Fair and nearly demolished in the 1970s, it reopened as a museum in 1986; trains called here for only 39 years, and its great station clock still looks over the main hall.

It began in 1824 when the British government bought 38 paintings from banker John Julius Angerstein's collection for £57,000; it now holds Van Gogh's Sunflowers and Turner's The Fighting Temeraire, and admission has always been free.
The gallery fills the former Bankside Power Station; its 99-metre chimney was kept just below the height of St Paul's dome across the river, and the old turbine hall below it runs 155 metres long.

Alfred Waterhouse clad the 1881 building in terracotta because it withstood London's soot; in the central hall a 25-metre blue whale skeleton named Hope has hung from the ceiling since 2017, in the spot long held by Dippy the Diplodocus cast.
Vasari built it from 1560 as offices, 'uffizi', for Cosimo I's magistrates, and the Medici soon filled the top floor with their collections; it holds Botticelli's The Birth of Venus and Primavera.

Its centrepiece, Rembrandt's The Night Watch, measures about 3.6 by 4.4 metres and closes the Gallery of Honour; a public passageway still runs straight through the 1885 Cuypers building, open to cyclists.

clue: Museum of Modern Art, United States 🇺🇸
fact: The first museum devoted to modern art opened in 1929, nine days after the Wall Street Crash; among its roughly 200,000 works is Van Gogh's The Starry Night, acquired in 1941.

Frank Lloyd Wright's museum took 16 years from commission to opening in October 1959, six months after his death; visitors ride the lift to the top and walk down one continuous spiral ramp about a quarter of a mile long.

clue: National Air and Space Museum, United States 🇺🇸
fact: Its entrance hall displays the original 1903 Wright Flyer and the Apollo 11 command module Columbia; the museum opened on the National Mall for the Bicentennial in 1976 and holds the largest collection of historic aircraft and spacecraft in the world.

clue: American Museum of Natural History, United States 🇺🇸
fact: Its halls hold tens of millions of specimens; the 29-metre blue whale model in the Hall of Ocean Life was modelled on a female whale caught off South America in 1925 and has hung there, in changing paint, since 1969.

clue: Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Israel 🇮🇱
fact: Consecrated in 335 over the sites of the Crucifixion and Christ's tomb, the church is shared by six Christian denominations under a centuries-old status quo so rigid that a wooden ladder on a ledge above its entrance has stood unmoved since the 1700s.

The world's tallest building from 2004 to 2010, it is steadied against typhoons and earthquakes by a 660-tonne steel pendulum suspended between its 87th and 92nd floors, the largest tuned mass damper on Earth.

Wren's cathedral, finished in 1710 on the ashes of the Great Fire, hides a structural brick cone between its inner and outer domes to carry the 850-ton lantern; it remained London's tallest building until 1963.
At 182 metres this statue of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel is the tallest in the world, twice the height of the Statue of Liberty; its viewing gallery sits in the chest, 153 metres up.

When it opened in 1883 it was the longest suspension bridge on Earth. Its chief engineer, Washington Roebling, crippled by caisson disease, directed the work through a telescope from a Brooklyn window while his wife Emily carried his instructions to the site.
At 634 metres the tallest tower in the world, its height is a pun: 6-3-4 can be read as 'Musashi', the old name of the province Tokyo stands in.
Begun in 1386 and not finished until 1965, this marble cathedral carries some 3,400 statues, more than any other building in the world, crowned by the gilded Madonnina of 1774.
Brunelleschi's dome, raised from 1420 with no scaffolding or wooden centring, is still the largest masonry dome ever built; a staircase climbs between its two shells to the lantern.
Shah Jahan's red sandstone palace-fortress, finished in 1648, is where India's prime minister raises the flag and addresses the nation every Independence Day, from the rampart above its Lahori Gate.

Opened in 1913, its main concourse ceiling paints the zodiac in reverse, defended by the Vanderbilts as the stars seen from God's viewpoint; the four-faced clock above the information booth is faced in opal.
Completed in 1902 on the triangular scrap where Broadway slices across Fifth Avenue, this steel-framed skyscraper narrows to a prow barely 2 metres wide at its point.
Its three 55-storey towers carry a single boat-shaped SkyPark whose 146-metre infinity pool floats some 190 metres above Marina Bay.

George Washington's Potomac estate, expanded under his eye for 45 years; its 'stone' mansion walls are actually pine boards rusticated with sand thrown onto wet paint, and Washington lies in the brick tomb he specified in his will.
Begun in 785 as a mosque, its hall marches away under more than 850 double-tiered red-and-white arches; after the city fell in 1236 a Gothic cathedral was planted in its exact centre.

Perched on an extinct volcano, the castle keeps Scotland's crown jewels and the Stone of Scone, returned from Westminster Abbey in 1996; its great cannon Mons Meg, a gift of 1457, hurled 150-kilogram stones over 3 km.
The Ottoman sultans' seat for nearly 400 years, its treasury holds the 86-carat Spoonmaker's Diamond, said to have been found by a fisherman and traded away for three spoons.
Nicknamed the Coathanger, its 1932 steel arch is pinned by 6 million rivets and breathes with the heat, the deck rising as much as 18 cm on the hottest days.

Toyotomi Hideyoshi raised Japan's grandest castle here in 1583; it fell to siege in 1615 and burned by lightning in 1665, and the white keep seen today is a 1931 concrete reconstruction paid for by the citizens of Osaka.
Installed in 1410, the Orloj is the oldest astronomical clock still working; its apostles parade on the hour, and legend says the city blinded its clockmaker so he could never build another.

Lutyens' 42-metre arch is cut with the names of more than 13,000 servicemen of the Indian Army who died in the First World War and the Third Anglo-Afghan War; an eternal flame burned beneath it from 1972 to 2022.

This 1377 border fortress is sold to the world as Dracula's castle, although Vlad the Impaler probably never lived here and Bram Stoker, who never visited Romania, modelled his fictional castle on its perch above the pass.

Built in 1799, the 'Palace of Winds' is a five-storey pink screen of 953 small latticed windows, raised so the royal women could watch street processions without being seen; behind the facade it is barely one room deep.
Headquarters of the Teutonic Order from 1309, this triple-walled brick fortress on the Nogat is the largest castle in the world by land area, built to house and feed some 3,000 brothers.
A flight of 272 rainbow-painted steps climbs to a cathedral-sized cave temple; beside it stands a 42.7-metre statue of Murugan, the tallest of that god anywhere, coated in 300 litres of gold paint.

Gaudí's 1906 rebuild for the Batlló family is nicknamed the House of Bones for its skeletal stone balconies; its roof is a dragon's arched, scale-tiled back, pierced by a turret bearing the cross of St George.

Rebuilt in stone in 1912 after fire destroyed its wooden predecessor, the Wodeyar palace is outlined by some 97,000 light bulbs during the Dasara festival, and the royal family still lives in one wing.
The largest Gothic cathedral in the world stands on Seville's great mosque, whose minaret survives as its bell tower, the Giralda; inside, four kings in stone carry the tomb of Christopher Columbus.

Venice's cathedral is clad in crusader loot: the four bronze horses over its facade were stolen from Constantinople in 1204, and its gold altarpiece, the Pala d'Oro, is studded with some 1,300 pearls.

The largest rainforest on Earth holds an estimated 390 billion individual trees across some 5.5 million km², about 60 percent of it in Brazil. About one in ten of all known species lives here, and its canopy drives weather far beyond South America: the forest exhales so much moisture that its “flying rivers” carry rain to farms thousands of kilometres south.

Once the world’s fourth-largest lake at about 68,000 km², the Aral has shrunk to roughly a tenth of that since the 1960s, when its two feeder rivers were diverted to irrigate cotton. Its old port of Muynak now sits over 100 km from the shore, its fishing fleet rusting in sand.

About a third of this island’s plant species grow nowhere else on Earth. Its umbrella-shaped dragon blood trees bleed a deep red resin that was traded across the ancient world as dye, medicine and varnish, and the island sat cut off from mainland Africa for millions of years, evolving in isolation.

North America’s driest desert is named for the Mohave people of the Colorado River. Its Joshua trees are giant yuccas that grow almost nowhere else, and at Kelso its dunes “sing”: avalanching sand on the slip faces hums and booms at up to about 105 decibels.

Europe’s busiest waterway runs 1,230 km from the Swiss Alps to Rotterdam, the continent’s largest port. Its 65 km Middle Rhine gorge is lined with more than 40 castles, and at the Lorelei rock the river narrows into its most storied and once most dangerous bend.

The longest river in western Asia, at about 2,800 km, is formed in Turkey where the Karasu and Murat streams join, and Babylon stood on its banks in what is now Iraq. At Qurna in the south it meets the Tigris, and the two flow on together as the Shatt al-Arab to the Gulf.

The river that carved the Grand Canyon is now so fully allocated among seven US states and Mexico that it rarely reaches its delta in the Gulf of California. In 2014 a deliberate “pulse flow” released from Morelos Dam reconnected it with the sea for the first time in decades.

At 3,767 km the Missouri is the longest river in North America, longer than the Mississippi it joins at St Louis. In 1805 Lewis and Clark spent about a month portaging its five Great Falls in Montana, hauling boats and gear some 18 miles overland around them.

This 2,285 m granite peak is traditionally identified as the mountain where Moses received the Ten Commandments. At its foot stands St Catherine’s Monastery, founded in the sixth century and still home to monks, beside the site pilgrims venerate as the Burning Bush.

At 8,586 m it is the third-highest mountain on Earth, and until surveys in 1852 it was thought to be the highest. Its name means “the five treasures of snow” for its five summits, and by a tradition honoured since the first ascent in 1955, climbers stop a few feet short of the very top.

The only Great Lake lying entirely inside the United States. In 1900 Chicago reversed the flow of its river to carry the city's sewage away from its drinking-water source, and the diversion still pulls roughly 2.1 billion gallons a day out of the lake under a Supreme Court decree.

fact: Huron holds Manitoulin Island, the largest island in any lake in the world, and its Georgian Bay is big enough to be sometimes counted as a sixth Great Lake. In the White Hurricane of November 1913, a single storm sank 12 ships on this lake and killed more than 250 sailors.

clue: Lake Erie, Canada and United States 🇨🇦🇺🇸
fact: The shallowest of the Great Lakes, Erie warms the fastest in summer, and farm runoff turns its western basin green with algal blooms. Off its western islands in 1813, Oliver Hazard Perry's American squadron defeated the British in the Battle of Lake Erie.

clue: Lake Ontario, Canada and United States 🇨🇦🇺🇸
fact: The smallest Great Lake by surface area is fed by the Niagara River and drains east through the St Lawrence River toward the Atlantic. It is deep for its size, 244 m at its deepest, and its surface seldom freezes across even in hard winters.
